claim: Cerebral malaria (CM) is responsible for a substantial proportion of the approximately 500,000 annual malaria deaths and 2,000,000 severe malaria cases.
source: Cerebral malaria (CM) is responsible for a substantial proportion of the approximately 500,000 annual malaria deaths and 2,000,000 severe malaria cases (WHO, 2014, WHO, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to WHO reports from 2014 and 2015.

claim: CM is defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as unarousable coma with circulating malaria (Plasmodium) parasitemia and no known non-malaria causal explanation.
source: CM is defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as unarousable coma with circulating malaria (Plasmodium) parasitemia and no known non-malaria causal explanation (WHO, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO 2000 defining cerebral malaria.

claim: Based on the presence or absence of malaria-specific retinal changes, CM can be classified as retinopathy-positive (Ret+) or retinopathy-negative (Ret-).
source: Based on the presence or absence of malaria-specific retinal changes, CM can be classified as retinopathy-positive (Ret+) or retinopathy-negative (Ret-) (Lewallen et al., 1999; Beare et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lewallen et al., 1999 and Beare et al., 2006.

claim: 40% of CM cases in the cohort were Ret-.
source: 40% of CM cases in our cohort were Ret-
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study cohort presented in the manuscript.

claim: Of Ret- CM cases, 12% died.
source: 40% of CM cases in our cohort were Ret- and of these, 12% died
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study cohort presented in the manuscript.

claim: Of Ret- CM cases, 10% developed neurological problems.
source: 40% of CM cases in our cohort were Ret- and of these, 12% died and 10% developed neurological problems (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study cohort presented in Table 1.

claim: Children dying of Ret+ CM have a high degree of sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in cerebral vasculature.
source: Autopsy data show that children dying of Ret+ CM have a high degree of sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in cerebral vasculature (Taylor et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to autopsy data from Taylor et al., 2004.

claim: Sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in cerebral vasculature is considered the pathological hallmark of CM.
source: Autopsy data show that children dying of Ret+ CM have a high degree of sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in cerebral vasculature (Taylor et al., 2004), considered the pathological hallmark of CM.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cerebral malaria pathology.

claim: Among children for whom retinopathy was assessed, 41 of 42 children dying with Ret+ CM had substantial cerebral sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in the cerebral microvasculature (defined as ≥23% of cerebral capillaries had sequestration).
source: among children for whom retinopathy was assessed, 41 of 42 children dying with Ret+ CM had substantial cerebral sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in the cerebral microvasculature (defined as ≥23% of cerebral capillaries had sequestration)
evidence: The claim is supported by autopsy data from Taylor et al. (2004) with follow-up results.

claim: Children dying with Ret+ CM mostly lacked other identified potential causes of death besides the malaria parasitemia.
source: 41 of 42 children dying with Ret+ CM had substantial cerebral sequestration of parasitized red blood cells in the cerebral microvasculature (defined as ≥23% of cerebral capillaries had sequestration) and mostly lacked other identified potential causes of death besides the malaria parasitemia
evidence: The claim is supported by autopsy data from Taylor et al. (2004) with follow-up results.

claim: All 15 children dying with Ret- CM lacked substantial cerebral sequestration (<23% of cerebral capillaries had sequestration).
source: all 15 children dying with Ret- CM lacked substantial cerebral sequestration (<23% of cerebral capillaries had sequestration)
evidence: The claim is supported by autopsy data from Taylor et al. (2004) with follow-up results.

claim: Children dying with Ret- CM mostly had non-malarial etiologies of death.
source: all 15 children dying with Ret- CM lacked substantial cerebral sequestration (<23% of cerebral capillaries had sequestration) and mostly had non-malarial etiologies of death (see Appendix 1 for causes of death)
evidence: The claim is supported by autopsy data from Taylor et al. (2004) with follow-up results.

claim: Incidental malaria parasitemia is common in people living in areas of high malaria transmission.
source: Incidental malaria parasitemia is common in people living in areas of high malaria transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about malaria epidemiology.

claim: It is possible that at least some children with Ret- CM have a non-malarial etiology of coma and an incidental (asymptomatic) malaria parasitemia.
source: Therefore, it is possible that at least some children with Ret- CM have a non-malarial etiology of coma and an incidental (asymptomatic) malaria parasitemia.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that incidental parasitemia is common.

claim: The pathogenesis of Ret-CM is unclear, and the role of malaria parasitemia in the etiology of the acute illness is unknown.
source: The pathogenesis of Ret-CM is therefore unclear, and the role of malaria parasitemia in the etiology of the acute illness is unknown (Postels and Birbeck, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Postels and Birbeck, 2011.

claim: A lower bound for the fraction of retinopathy-negative CM that would be prevented if malaria parasitemia were to be eliminated is estimated to be 0.93 (95% confidence interval: 0.68, 1).
source: A lower bound for the fraction of retinopathy-negative CM that would be prevented if malaria parasitemia were to be eliminated is estimated to be 0.93 (95% confidence interval: 0.68, 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: There are 3704 community controls in the study.
source: There are 3704 community controls, but their characteristics are not shown because only their genotypes and not their clinical characteristics were collected.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The Blantyre coma score is statistically significantly higher in Ret+ CM patients than Ret- CM patients.
source: The Blantyre coma score is statistically significantly higher in Ret+ CM patients than Ret- CM patients
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data presented in Table 1.

claim: The difference in Blantyre coma score between Ret+ CM and Ret- CM patients is not clinically significant.
source: The Blantyre coma score is statistically significantly higher in Ret+ CM patients than Ret- CM patients, but we do not regard the difference as clinically significant.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of the clinical significance of the statistical difference.

claim: Patients with Ret+ CM were more severely ill than those with Ret- CM.
source: In general, the patients with Ret+ CM were more severely ill than those with Ret- CM (higher lactate, more deep breathing and a higher chance of death).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing higher lactate, more deep breathing, and higher mortality in Ret+ CM.

claim: The malaria illness is more severe in Ret+ CM than Ret- CM patients.
source: The malaria illness is more severe in Ret+ CM than Ret- CM patients (lower platelet count and more anemia).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing lower platelet count and more anemia in Ret+ CM.

claim: The higher opening CSF pressures in Ret+ CM patients compared to Ret- CM patients suggests a higher proportion of Ret+CM patients have increased brain volume.
source: The higher opening CSF pressures in Ret+ CM patients compared to Ret- CM patients suggests a higher proportion of Ret+CM patients have increased brain volume.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed difference in CSF opening pressures between groups.

claim: Laboratory abnormalities associated with malaria infection (e.g. low hematocrit and platelet count) were more frequent in the CM cases compared to non-malaria controls.
source: Comparing CM cases to non-malaria controls, as expected, laboratory abnormalities associated with malaria infection (e.g. low hematocrit and platelet count) were more frequent in the CM cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1.

claim: The sickle cell trait (HbAS) protects against symptomatic malaria.
source: The sickle cell trait (HbAS) – inheritance of one abnormal allele of the betaglobin gene – protects against symptomatic malaria (Modiano et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2012; Williams et al., 2005; Willcox et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Blood group O protects against CM compared to groups A, B or AB.
source: A second inherited trait which affects susceptibility to malaria illness is blood group O (BGO), which protects against CM compared to groups A, B or AB (Cserti and Dzik, 2007; Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: For both BGO and HbAS, it is plausible that the traits do not protect against malaria parasitemia incidence as systematic reviews have not found consistent evidence for protection.
source: For both BGO and HbAS, it is plausible that the traits do not protect against malaria parasitemia incidence as systematic reviews have not found consistent evidence for protection (Uneke, 2007; Taylor et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to systematic reviews.

claim: Non-malaria hospitalized controls did not differ from community controls for HbAS (p-value=0.86).
source: For both HbAS and BGO, non-malaria hospitalized controls did not differ from community controls (HbAS p-value=0.86
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Non-malaria hospitalized controls did not differ from community controls for BGO (p-value=0.83).
source: For both HbAS and BGO, non-malaria hospitalized controls did not differ from community controls (HbAS p-value=0.86; BGO p-value=0.83)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Controls had a higher proportion of HbAS than true Ret- CM patients (odds ratio: 14.33, 95% CI: 3.21, 257.24).
source: Controls had a higher proportion of HbAS than true Ret- CM patients (odds ratio: 14.33, 95% CI: 3.21, 257.24)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Controls had a higher proportion of HbAS than true Ret+ CM patients (odds ratio: 1223.22, 95% CI: 9.87,∞).
source: Controls had a higher proportion of HbAS than true Ret- CM patients (odds ratio: 14.33, 95% CI: 3.21, 257.24) and true Ret+ CM patients (odds ratio: 1223.22, 95% CI: 9.87,∞).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: For BGO, the controls were comparable to true Ret- CM patients (odds ratio: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.83, 1.29).
source: For BGO, the controls were comparable to true Ret- CM patients (odds ratio: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.83, 1.29)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: For BGO, the controls had a higher proportion than true Ret+ CM patients (odds ratio: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.50).
source: For BGO, the controls were comparable to true Ret- CM patients (odds ratio: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.83, 1.29) but higher than true Ret+ CM patients (odds ratio: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.50).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: There is strong evidence to reject the null hypothesis that HbAS frequency is the same in controls and true Ret- CM cases (p-value<0.0001).
source: There is strong evidence to reject H0HbAS(p-value<0.0001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: There is not evidence to reject the null hypothesis that BGO frequency is the same in controls and true Ret- CM cases (p-value=0.79).
source: There is strong evidence to reject H0HbAS(p-value<0.0001) but not H0BGO (p-value=0.79)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Malaria parasitemia is pathogenic for a proportion of Ret- CM cases.
source: Taken together, these tests suggest that malaria parasitemia is pathogenic for a proportion of Ret- CM cases.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the statistical tests showing HbAS protection but not BGO protection for Ret- CM.

claim: Sickle cell trait protects against Ret- CM.
source: Sickle cell trait protects against Ret- CM, but blood group O does not.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Blood group O does not protect against Ret- CM.
source: Sickle cell trait protects against Ret- CM, but blood group O does not.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Under the main model that assumes the traits do not protect against malaria parasitemia incidence, the lower bound on malaria parasitemia attributable fraction of Ret- CM is estimated to be .93 with 95% confidence interval (.68, 1).
source: Under the main model, the lower bound is estimated to be .93 with 95% confidence interval (.68, 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data under the main model assumptions.

claim: Under all sensitivity analysis scenarios considered, lower 95% confidence bounds for the malaria parasitemia attributable fraction ranged from .37 to .77.
source: Under all scenarios considered, we found evidence for a substantial contribution of malaria parasites to the pathogenesis of Ret- CM with lower 95% confidence bounds ranging from .37 to .77
evidence: The claim is supported by sensitivity analyses presented in Table 3.

claim: Under all sensitivity analysis scenarios considered, point estimates for the lower bound on malaria parasitemia attributable fraction ranged from .86 to .95.
source: Under all scenarios considered, we found evidence for a substantial contribution of malaria parasites to the pathogenesis of Ret- CM with lower 95% confidence bounds ranging from .37 to .77 and point estimates for the lower bound ranging from .86 to .95.
evidence: The claim is supported by sensitivity analyses presented in Table 3.

claim: Children with genetic traits associated with resistance to malaria illness are underrepresented in admissions with both Ret+ and Ret- CM (HbAS).
source: We have studied a natural experiment that alters the level of malaria illness and found evidence that children with genetic traits associated with resistance to malaria illness are underrepresented in admissions with both Ret+ and Ret- CM (HbAS)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Children with genetic traits associated with resistance to malaria illness are underrepresented in admissions with Ret+ CM only (BGO).
source: We have studied a natural experiment that alters the level of malaria illness and found evidence that children with genetic traits associated with resistance to malaria illness are underrepresented in admissions with both Ret+ and Ret- CM (HbAS) or in admissions with Ret+ CM only (BGO).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: HbAS protects children with malaria parasitemia from developing uncomplicated malaria illness (e.g., fever) and severe malaria illness.
source: HbAS protects children with malaria parasitemia from developing uncomplicated malaria illness (e.g., fever) and severe malaria illness (Taylor et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2012.

claim: Current evidence suggests that BGO has no effect on developing uncomplicated malaria illness.
source: By contrast, current evidence suggests that BGO has no effect on developing uncomplicated malaria illness (Uneke, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uneke, 2007.

claim: BGO inhibits the cytoadherence of parasitized red blood cells to endothelial cells in the microcirculation.
source: By contrast, current evidence suggests that BGO has no effect on developing uncomplicated malaria illness (Uneke, 2007), but does inhibit the cytoadherence of parasitized red blood cells to endothelial cells in the microcirculation, e.g., by affecting rosetting (Rowe et al., 2007) and physical properties of the red cell membrane (Méndez et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rowe et al., 2007 and Méndez et al., 2012.

claim: BGO prevents severe malaria illness.
source: but does inhibit the cytoadherence of parasitized red blood cells to endothelial cells in the microcirculation, e.g., by affecting rosetting (Rowe et al., 2007) and physical properties of the red cell membrane (Méndez et al., 2012), thereby preventing severe malaria illness (Cserti and Dzik, 2007; Migot-Nabias et al., 2000; Uneke, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: There is evidence for interaction between malaria parasites and other pathogens.
source: While the interactions between malaria parasites and other pathogens are incompletely understood and not well investigated, there is evidence for interaction (Obaro and Greenwood, 2011; Mallewa et al., 2013; Postels and Birbeck, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The effect of microvascular parasite sequestration on the integrity of the gut mucosa is thought to allow bacterial seeding into the blood stream and hence bacteremia.
source: In studies of sepsis and malaria, the effect of microvascular parasite sequestration on the integrity of the gut mucosa is thought to allow bacterial seeding into the blood stream and hence bacteremia (Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scott et al., 2011.

claim: Following antigenic challenge from a Plasmodium falciparum candidate vaccine, children coinfected with schistosomiasis had lower acquired specific immune responses than those not infected.
source: Another example is that following antigenic challenge from a Plasmodium falciparum candidate vaccine, children coinfected with schistosomiasis had lower acquired specific immune responses than those not infected (Diallo et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Diallo et al., 2010.

claim: Among children dying from Ret- CM, malaria parasitemia is typically not the sole cause of death.
source: Taylor et al. (2004)'s autopsy study results suggest that among children dying from Ret- CM, malaria parasitemia is typically not the sole cause of death (see Causes of Death in Autopsy study in Appendix 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to autopsy data from Taylor et al., 2004.

claim: It is possible that in survivors from Ret- CM, malaria parasitemia is the major contributor to acute illness.
source: but it is possible that in survivors from Ret- CM, malaria parasitemia is the major contributor to acute illness.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about survivors of Ret- CM.

claim: Whether malarial retinopathy is present or absent in CM could be affected by factors such as the child's genome, the parasite's genome and the child's previous exposures to malaria.
source: Whether malarial retinopathy is present or absent in CM could be affected by factors such as the child's genome, the parasite's genome and the child's previous exposures to malaria (Postels and Birbeck, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Postels and Birbeck, 2011.

claim: The protection provided against Ret- CM by HbAS but not BGO could be explained by an interaction between the factor(s) affecting whether malarial retinopathy is present and BGO.
source: The protection provided against Ret- CM by HbAS but not BGO could be explained by an interaction between the factor(s) affecting whether malarial retinopathy is present and BGO, e.g., a parasite genotype which causes malarial retinopathy to be absent could interfere with the mechanism by which BGO provides protection against severe malaria.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: Adult and pediatric CM have important clinical differences.
source: Adult and pediatric CM have important clinical differences and our results may not be generalizable to adults with Ret- CM.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about cerebral malaria.

claim: The results of this study may not be generalizable to adults with Ret- CM.
source: Adult and pediatric CM have important clinical differences and our results may not be generalizable to adults with Ret- CM.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the limitations of the study's generalizability.

claim: Detection of the presence or absence of malarial retinopathy was determined by several ophthalmologists over the 11 year duration of data collection.
source: Detection of the presence or absence of malarial retinopathy was determined by several ophthalmologists over the 11 year duration of data collection
evidence: The claim describes the study methodology.

claim: The sensitivity of detection of retinal changes may have varied between practitioners.
source: Detection of the presence or absence of malarial retinopathy was determined by several ophthalmologists over the 11 year duration of data collection, the sensitivity of detection of retinal changes may have varied between practitioners.
evidence: The claim is an inference about potential variability in the study methodology.

claim: Malarial retinopathy was determined on the basis of ophthalmoscopy alone.
source: Malarial retinopathy was determined on the basis of ophthalmoscopy alone
evidence: The claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Techniques such as optical coherence tomography may increase sensitivity for detecting malarial retinopathy.
source: but since the time of our study, techniques such as optical coherence tomography that may increase sensitivity have been developed (Joshi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joshi et al., 2017.

claim: Malarial retinopathy is measured at the time of admission.
source: We measure malarial retinopathy at the time of admission, but patients are admitted at different points on the disease trajectory.
evidence: The claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Patients are admitted at different points on the disease trajectory.
source: We measure malarial retinopathy at the time of admission, but patients are admitted at different points on the disease trajectory.
evidence: The claim is an observation about the study design.

claim: Malarial retinopathy can change over time.
source: Malarial retinopathy can change over time; it doesn't resolve during the 2–4 days of hospitalization but can become worse, which is a poor prognostic sign.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical knowledge about malarial retinopathy.

claim: Malarial retinopathy doesn't resolve during the 2–4 days of hospitalization.
source: Malarial retinopathy can change over time; it doesn't resolve during the 2–4 days of hospitalization but can become worse, which is a poor prognostic sign.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical knowledge about malarial retinopathy.

claim: Malarial retinopathy can become worse during hospitalization, which is a poor prognostic sign.
source: Malarial retinopathy can change over time; it doesn't resolve during the 2–4 days of hospitalization but can become worse, which is a poor prognostic sign.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical knowledge about malarial retinopathy.

claim: The main analysis assumed that possession of HbAS or BGO does not affect malaria parasitemia incidence.
source: Our main analysis assumed that possession of HbAS or BGO does not affect malaria parasitemia incidence
evidence: The claim describes an assumption of the main analysis.

claim: Sensitivity analyses showed that the results were not sensitive to plausible violations of the assumption that HbAS or BGO does not affect malaria parasitemia incidence.
source: Our main analysis assumed that possession of HbAS or BGO does not affect malaria parasitemia incidence; however, sensitivity analyses showed that our results were not sensitive to plausible violations of this assumption.
evidence: The claim is supported by sensitivity analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The analysis assumed that HbAS and BGO do not have selection effects on which CM cases are admitted to the Paediatric Research Ward as opposed to dying before reaching the Paedieatric Research Ward or being cured before needing to be referred to the ward.
source: Our analysis assumed that HbAS and BGO do not have selection effects on which CM cases are admitted to the Paediatric Research Ward as opposed to dying before reaching the Paedieatric Research Ward or being cured before needing to be referred to the ward
evidence: The claim describes an assumption of the analysis.

claim: Some of the non-malaria hospital controls had malaria parasitemia.
source: Some of the non-malaria hospital controls had malaria parasitemia
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: It is possible that malaria contributed to the illness in some non-malaria hospital control participants.
source: Some of the non-malaria hospital controls had malaria parasitemia; since children can sometimes develop severe malaria with relatively low levels of parasitemia, it is possible that malaria contributed to the illness in these control participants.
evidence: The claim is an inference about potential confounding in the control group.

claim: Older non-malaria hospital controls may have a selection bias for HbAS since they have survived to an older age.
source: Furthermore, older non-malaria hospital controls may have a selection bias for HbAS since they have survived to an older age (Ackerman et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by a citation to Ackerman et al., 2005.

claim: The study sample includes children with WHO-defined CM from 1997 to 2007 who were admitted to the Paediatric Research Ward at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital.
source: The study sample includes children with WHO-defined CM from 1997 to 2007 who were admitted to the Paediatric Research Ward at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, a tertiary referral center and teaching hospital in Blantyre, Malawi.
evidence: The claim describes the study sample and setting.

claim: Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital is a tertiary referral center and teaching hospital in Blantyre, Malawi.
source: The study sample includes children with WHO-defined CM from 1997 to 2007 who were admitted to the Paediatric Research Ward at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, a tertiary referral center and teaching hospital in Blantyre, Malawi.
evidence: The claim describes the study setting.

claim: Patients were enrolled during the rainy season, the time of annual peak incidence of CM.
source: Patients were enrolled during the rainy season, the time of annual peak incidence of CM.
evidence: The claim describes the study enrollment period.

claim: All patients were treated with intravenous quinine as standard antimalarial therapy.
source: All patients were treated with intravenous quinine as standard antimalarial therapy.
evidence: The claim describes the treatment protocol.

claim: Enrollment in the study required explicit written consent from the parent or guardian.
source: Enrollment in the study required explicit written consent from the parent or guardian.
evidence: The claim describes the study consent process.

claim: There were 947 enrolled patients.
source: There were 947 enrolled patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Malarial retinopathy was assessed on 726 of the 947 enrolled patients.
source: Malarial retinopathy was assessed on 726 of these patients and we subsequently limited our analysis to these 726 patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The analysis was limited to the 726 patients on whom malarial retinopathy was assessed.
source: Malarial retinopathy was assessed on 726 of these patients and we subsequently limited our analysis to these 726 patients.
evidence: The claim describes the study sample selection.

claim: Direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy were performed by an ophthalmologist well versed in findings typical of malarial retinopathy.
source: To assess retinal changes, direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy were performed by an ophthalmologist well versed in findings typical of malarial retinopathy.
evidence: The claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Community controls were cord blood samples from Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, mostly from the newborn nursery.
source: Community controls were cord blood samples from Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, mostly from the newborn nursery.
evidence: The claim describes the source of community controls.

claim: Hospital controls were 194 patients who were admitted during the study period to the Paediatric Research Ward at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital with a non-malarial cause of illness – meningitis, non-malarial anemia or other non-malaria illness.
source: The second type of controls are 194 patients who were admitted during the study period to the Paediatric Research Ward at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital with a non-malarial cause of illness – meningitis, non-malarial anemia or other non-malaria illness.
evidence: The claim describes the hospital control group.

claim: If two control groups have similar exposure rates, this provides evidence against hidden bias and selection bias.
source: If two such control groups have similar exposure rates, this provides evidence against hidden bias and selection bias (Rosenbaum, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rosenbaum, 1987.

claim: If the case group has a different exposure rate than both control groups and the control groups have similar exposure rates, this provides stronger evidence that the exposure has a causal effect on the outcome, rather than the results being biased by hidden bias or selection bias, as compared to a study with a single control group.
source: Further, if the case group has a different exposure rate than both control groups and the control groups have similar exposure rates, this provides stronger evidence that the exposure has a causal effect on the outcome, rather than the results being biased by hidden bias or selection bias, as compared to a study with a single control group (Rosenbaum, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rosenbaum, 1987.

claim: Community controls are less likely to suffer from selection bias than the hospital controls.
source: Community controls are less likely to suffer from selection bias than the hospital controls.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the relative bias in different control groups.

claim: Community controls were randomly selected from the same population as the cases.
source: Community controls were randomly selected from the same population as the cases.
evidence: The claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Hospital controls could suffer from selection bias if the genetic variant of interest was associated with a non-malaria illness.
source: In contrast, hospital controls could suffer from selection bias if the genetic variant of interest was associated with a non-malaria illness -- this type of selection bias is known as Berkson's bias (Westreich, 2012; Berkson, 1946).
evidence: The claim is an inference about potential bias supported by citations to Westreich, 2012 and Berkson, 1946.

claim: Hospital controls have the potential advantage that they would reduce hidden bias if there was population stratification such that the genetic variant was associated with an unmeasured population stratification feature that caused both malaria and non-malaria illness.
source: Although the hospital controls might suffer from more selection bias than the community controls, the hospital controls have the potential advantage that they would reduce hidden bias if there was population stratification such that the genetic variant was associated with an unmeasured population stratification feature (e.g., housing conditions) that caused both malaria and non-malaria illness.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the potential advantages of hospital controls.

claim: Participants were genotyped using the Sequenom iPLEX MassARRAY platform.
source: Participants were genotyped using the Sequenom iPLEX MassARRAY platform (Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network, 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the genotyping methodology and is supported by a citation.

claim: The genotyping included 55 SNPs for which there were previously reported associations with severe malaria.
source: The genotyping included 55 SNPs for which there were previously reported associations with severe malaria.
evidence: The claim describes the genotyping methodology.

claim: Two of the SNPs were found to be statistically significantly (p<.05) associated with cerebral malaria in Malawi -- HBB rs334, which encodes the sickle cell trait, and ABO rs8176719, which encodes the blood type (O vs. A, B or AB).
source: Two of the SNPs were found to be statistically significantly (p<.05) associated with cerebral malaria in Malawi -- HBB rs334, which encodes the sickle cell trait, and ABO rs8176719, which encodes the blood type (O vs. A, B or AB); see Figure 1 in Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network (2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and a citation to Malaria Genomic Epidemiology Network (2014).

claim: HBB rs334 encodes the sickle cell trait.
source: HBB rs334, which encodes the sickle cell trait
evidence: The claim is based on established genetic knowledge.

claim: ABO rs8176719 encodes the blood type (O vs. A, B or AB).
source: ABO rs8176719, which encodes the blood type (O vs. A, B or AB)
evidence: The claim is based on established genetic knowledge.

claim: Sickle cell trait is underrepresented in patients with Ret+ and Ret- cerebral malaria (CM) because of the bottleneck at the transition between 'malaria infection' (asymptomatic malaria) and 'malaria disease' (uncomplicated malaria).
source: Sickle cell trait is underrepresented in patients with Ret+ and Ret- cerebral malaria (CM) because of the bottleneck at the transition between 'malaria infection' (asymptomatic malaria) and 'malaria disease' (uncomplicated malaria).
evidence: The claim is shown in Figure 1 and is an inference from the study results.

claim: Blood group O is underrepresented in patients with Ret+ CM, but not in those with Ret- CM.
source: Blood group O is underrepresented in patients with Ret+ CM, but not in those with Ret- CM.
evidence: The claim is shown in Figure 1 and is supported by the study results.

claim: The results for sickle cell trait and blood group O suggest that some Ret- CM cases occur through pathway (b).
source: Taken together, the results for sickle cell trait and blood group O suggest that some Ret- CM cases occur through pathway (b) (because sickle cell trait is underrepresented in Ret- CM)
evidence: The claim is an inference from the study results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Malaria parasites contribute to the pathogenesis of Ret- CM cases that occur through pathway (b).
